title: A Tiny Black Hole Could Unlock the Universe's Biggest Mystery!
summary: Imagine a black hole smaller than the Sun—so tiny it shouldn't exist! That's what a giant detector called LIGO might have found. Last year, LIGO sensed ripples in space from two objects crashing together. One of them was weirdly light, less than the mass of our Sun. Normal black holes come from exploding stars and are much heavier. So what was it? Scientists at the University of Miami think it could be a primordial black hole. These are special black holes that formed right after the Big Bang, when the universe was a hot, dense soup. They could be as small as an asteroid! No one has ever proven they exist. But if they do, they might solve a huge puzzle: dark matter. Dark matter is invisible stuff that makes up about 85% of all matter in the universe. It's like a hidden glue that keeps galaxies from flying apart. "Our research indicates that these primordial black holes could account for a significant portion, if not all, of dark matter," said Professor Nico Cappelluti. But scientists need more proof. One signal isn't enough. They're waiting for LIGO to catch more of these tiny black hole crashes. If it does, we might finally understand what most of the universe is made of!
why_it_matters: Finding out what dark matter really is could change how we understand the universe, and even help us know more about how galaxies like our Milky Way stay together.

background_read: LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) is a special machine that measures tiny ripples in space caused by crashing black holes.
Scientists think that right after the Big Bang (the explosion that started the universe), small black holes called primordial black holes might have formed.
Professor Nico Cappelluti from the University of Miami (a university in Florida) believes these tiny black holes could be the invisible dark matter that holds galaxies together.
Article_Structure: WHO: Professor Nico Cappelluti and his team at the University of Miami, along with LIGO scientists.
WHAT: LIGO picked up a signal from a black hole lighter than the Sun, possibly a primordial black hole that could be part of dark matter.
WHERE: The discovery involved LIGO’s detectors in the United States and analysis at the University of Miami.
WHY: Scientists want to solve the mystery of dark matter, the invisible stuff that makes up most of the universe.

perspectives.description: They believe this could be the first real clue to finally solve the dark matter mystery.
They warn that a single signal might just be an accident, so they need to see many more similar crashes before they can be sure.
For someone who loves space, it’s exciting to imagine that unknown objects like primordial black holes might be floating all around us.
